transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno, Priya Shah (Redwood); Jordan Li, Maya Chen, Carlos Ruiz (BrightScale)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive focusing on throughput tuning for BrightScale's inference workload. Covered continuous batching behavior, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch), token limits, KV cache reuse, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem considerations. Agreed to run targeted benchmarks with BrightScale sample payload and schedule on-prem pilot.

Topics:
- Continuous batching and scheduler parameters
- max_num_seqs and priority for short vs long requests
- token limits and tail-latency controls
- KV cache reuse for repeated prefixes
- 4-bit quant vs fp16 tradeoffs for latency/cost
- VPC/on-prem setup concerns and network egress

Transcript:
00:00:04 Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining; quick roll call?
00:00:10 Jordan: Jordan here - Platform eng at BrightScale.
00:00:12 Maya: Maya, SRE.
00:00:14 Carlos: Carlos, PM.
00:00:18 Priya: Priya from Redwood, SE. Alex, you wanna start?
00:00:22 Alex: Yeah, thanks. Today we wanted to go deeper on throughput tuning for your gen-text pipeline — I know you're ramping to 2k qps at peak and want predictable p99 latency. We'll walk through continuous batching knobs and some suggestions for the pilot.
00:00:38 Jordan: Yeah that's right, current targets are about 2k qps, average prompt ~60 tokens but we have a heavy tail to 800 tokens for long-form. Latency SLO is p99 < 450ms if possible, but we're flexible on p50.
00:00:50 Priya: Got it. Two big levers: batching and kv cache. Continuous batching increases throughput by aggregating requests, but it can add latency for single-shot short prompts if the scheduler waits for a batch window. We'll talk about max_num_seqs and token-based batch limits.
00:01:08 Maya: Can you clarify max_num_seqs? We saw it in the docs but not sure the exact impact.
00:01:12 Priya: Sure, max_num_seqs is basically the max number of sequences the scheduler will pack into a single GPU batch. So if you set max_num_seqs=8, the runtime will try to combine up to 8 simultaneous requests into one forward pass. For short prompts that's great; for long prompts you also need to cap max_total_tokens or max_tokens_per_batch because one 800-token request can dominate memory.
00:01:38 Jordan: So do we set it relative to GPU memory? We use A100 80GB for dedicated.
00:01:44 Priya: Exactly. For A100-80, with an LLM like an open-llama-70b equivalent quantized to 4-bit, we commonly see safe batch widths of 6-10 for avg prompt lengths ~60 tokens. But if you have a mix, a dynamic scheduler with token budget is better: set max_num_seqs=12 but max_total_tokens_per_batch=3200, so the scheduler will pack requests until token budget or seq limit triggers.
00:02:10 Alex: Also continuous batching has a latency_config: max_wait_ms. If you set max_wait_ms low (e.g. 8-12ms), you prioritize latency; higher values (30-50ms) increase throughput but add base latency.
00:02:23 Maya: What's our tradeoff point to keep p99 under 450ms?
00:02:28 Priya: With your traffic mix, I'd recommend max_wait_ms=20ms, max_num_seqs=10, max_total_tokens_per_batch=3600 as a starting point. That biases throughput but keeps short-request latency reasonable. We'll validate with your payload.
00:02:43 Carlos: How does KV caching play into this? We have many repeated prefixes — the system might benefit a lot.
00:02:48 Priya: KV caching is a major win for repeated prefixes. If your clients reuse history or system prompts, enable prefix caching and long-lived KV caches. The runtime will reuse cached key-values across requests so the forward pass for the prefix is skipped, saving compute and improving latency. Note: cache hit rate and TTL matter; if you have many slightly different prefixes, hit rate drops.
00:03:10 Jordan: Any gotchas for caching with quantized models?
00:03:14 Priya: Not much — the cache stores activations not weights. But quantization makes the model memory footprint smaller, so you can hold more KV cache in GPU memory. However, with 4-bit kernels we recommend validating numeric stability for very long contexts.
00:03:31 Maya: Regarding quantization — we want to reduce cost. Is 4-bit safe for production?
00:03:36 Priya: 4-bit (awq/ltq style) is common in production for many use cases. It gives big memory/speed wins at modest quality loss. For high-regression-sensitivity tasks you might prefer fp16. Best practice: run quality hook evals and compare top-k outputs, and if small regressions are acceptable, 4-bit is good. We'll provide suggested quant profiles.
00:03:58 Alex: Important: schedule separate lanes for short vs long requests. Short-request pool can have smaller max_wait_ms and smaller max_num_seqs; long-request pool can be optimized for throughput with larger max_total_tokens_per_batch.
00:04:12 Jordan: How do we route by request type? We have user-facing chat and background summarization.
00:04:18 Priya: Use route tags and the smart routing policy. Tag requests at the API level (e.g., route=chat_short or route=summarize_long). Then Redwood routing can apply pools with different scheduler knobs.
00:04:29 Carlos: What about tail latency when a long request gets in a mixed batch?
00:04:33 Priya: That's why token-budget batching is key. If a long request would push the batch token count too high, the scheduler will start a new batch for it; prevents long requests from inflating latency for short ones.
00:04:45 Maya: Are there kernel-level knobs? Our infra team cares about occupancy and kernel fusion.
00:04:51 Priya: The runtime auto-selects kernels based on seq length distribution, but you can hint via preferred_kernel and enable kernel_fusion optimizations. For dense long-context workloads, fused kernels help. We'll share kernel hints and profiling output.
00:05:06 Jordan: We saw the term "continuous batching mode" in the docs. What's the difference vs fixed-window batching?
00:05:12 Priya: Continuous batching adaptively collects requests as they arrive and packs them into ongoing batches; it doesn't force fixed windows. Fixed-window waits for a timer boundary. Continuous is usually better for variable arrival patterns; it's more responsive at low qps while still achieving high throughput at high qps. But it's slightly more complex to tune.
00:05:31 Alex: Quick note on max_num_seqs vs max_batch_size: in some places people confuse them. max_batch_size is the GPU-side maximum (memory limit). max_num_seqs is how many logical sequences the scheduler will attempt to pack. They interact but tuning both is necessary.
00:05:47 Carlos: Token limits — how do we protect from exploding token requests?
00:05:51 Priya: Set per-request token cap (max_input_tokens and max_output_tokens), and also set max_total_tokens_per_batch and max_tokens_per_seq. Also enable stream_timeouts to drop runaway requests.
00:06:05 Maya: For VPC and on-prem: any network implications for throughput?
00:06:09 Priya: Yes, on-prem network can add egress latency to the control plane if not colocated. For VPC-private deployments, we recommend placing the inference nodes in the same region and using private link for the control plane. Also pre-warm connections and tune NGINX/gRPC keepalive for high qps.
00:06:28 Jordan: If we do private deployment in our datacenter, can we run the same continuous batching runtime?
00:06:32 Priya: Yes — Redwood Private runs the same runtime. You'll need the Recommended GPU configuration and the container images. For on-prem we provide a deployment manifest and a couple of helper scripts to tune kernel flags and batch sizes. We'll help during the pilot.
00:06:45 Carlos: How do we measure success? What metrics should we report back?
00:06:48 Priya: Key metrics: p50/p90/p99 latency per route, tokens/sec per GPU, GPU utilization, batch sizes distribution, cache hit rate, and cost per 1M tokens. Also measure failed requests and queue_depth distribution.
00:07:04 Alex: We'll send a benchmark CSV template. Priya, can you outline the baseline set of experiments?
00:07:09 Priya: Sure. 1) Baseline single-client at your avg prompt: measure p50/p99 with no batching. 2) Continuous batching sweep: vary max_wait_ms (5, 10, 20, 40ms) and max_num_seqs (4,8,12) to see tradeoffs. 3) Token-budget sweep: set max_total_tokens_per_batch at 2400, 3600, 4800. 4) KV cache on/off to quantify hit-rate improvements. 5) Quantization: fp16 vs 4-bit. We'll produce a matrix and recommended baseline.
00:07:44 Jordan: That sounds good. For our long form tasks, do we need to reserve dedicated nodes?
00:07:48 Priya: If you have sustained long-context workloads that are memory heavy, dedicating a pool for them helps with predictable throughput and avoids noisy neighbors on shared pools. Dedicated also gives you reserved GPU memory and fixed throughput.
00:08:00 Maya: Autoscaling interaction — if nodes spin up, do caches warm immediately?
00:08:06 Priya: New nodes will have cold caches; there is a warm-up period. For best behavior, use sticky routing for sessions or keep a small warm pool to absorb traffic during scale-up. Also enable prefix prefetching for very common prompts.
00:08:20 Carlos: Any pitfalls with prefetching?
00:08:23 Priya: Prefetching increases memory use; don't prefetch excessively. Use it for a small set of top-k frequent prefixes.
00:08:30 Jordan: You mentioned max_num_seqs interacting with sequence padding overhead. Can you explain?
00:08:34 Priya: Yes — the runtime packs sequences of varying lengths, but the GPU costs are dominated by the longest sequence in the batch (padding). So packing several short sequences with one long one can hurt per-token efficiency. Token-budget batching reduces this by limiting total tokens, so long sequences either form their own batch or are grouped with other longs.
00:08:55 Maya: For our dataset, we have many short requests and occasional long ones — your earlier recommended knobs should handle it.
00:09:01 Priya: Right. One more thing: set per-route circuit-breakers to fallback to smaller models when latency spikes, and enable graceful degradation policies.
00:09:11 Carlos: Competitor question — how does Redwood's continuous batching compare to, say, Anthropic-hosted endpoints?
00:09:16 Priya: Other providers use batching too, but Redwood exposes more knobs and gives you per-route control and the same runtime across hosted/dedicated/private. That makes it easier to replicate production behavior across environments.
00:09:28 Alex: Ok let's walk through the initial benchmark plan and timeline.
00:09:32 Priya: Timeline: provision test cluster (Priya) by 2026-11-07, BrightScale to provide payload by 2026-11-10, run baselines and sweeps by 2026-11-12, review results week of 2026-11-15 and plan on-prem pilot.
00:09:48 Jordan: Fine. A couple random clarifying Qs: how fine-grained can we set max_wait_ms? Millisecond-level?
00:09:53 Priya: Yes, we support ms granularity, typical values 5-50ms. Also you can set adaptive_wait where the runtime reduces wait when load increases.
00:10:02 Maya: Logging and observability — can we get token-level breakdowns?
00:10:06 Priya: Yes, Redwood Console exposes per-token cost, per-route latencies, and batch-level traces. We can add custom tracing hooks into your traces for correlation ids.
00:10:16 Carlos: Any recommended defaults for A100-80 with 70B style models?
00:10:20 Priya: Defaults: max_num_seqs=8-10, max_total_tokens_per_batch=3200-3600, max_wait_ms=15-20ms, keep a warm pool of 1-2 nodes for scale events, and enable KV caching with TTL 10-30 minutes depending on your session reuse. Use 4-bit for cost-sensitive paths after QA.
00:10:40 Jordan: Great. A few of our infra folks will join the pilot kickoff.
00:10:44 Alex: We'll send an invite. Any final topics?
00:10:47 Maya: Kernel profiling — can Redwood share nvprof traces or flame graphs?
00:10:51 Priya: Yes, we'll share profiling output and suggested kernel flags; note that on-prem profilers vary but we'll provide guidance.
00:10:58 Carlos: Ok let's summarize next steps.
00:11:02 Alex: Recap: Priya runs infra and benchmarks; Jordan provides payload; Alex shares pricing/throughput sheet; schedule pilot.
00:11:10 Jordan: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
00:11:12 Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up with calendar and artifacts.
